title: When the Atlas Breaks
premise: In the winter of 1917, Silas Fairweather, a battlefield nurse who secretly records in his ledger the names of soldiers that official reports omit, is stranded when the only bridge out of the river valley closes for the season. He takes refuge at a decaying mapmaking workshop, the Atlas House, where he discovers his late mother's connection to its eccentric owner, Odile Marchand, and her ward, a deserter named Tomas. As the workshop faces demolition orders and Silas's ledger becomes evidence of a cover-up, he must choose between escaping with his own name restored and staying to finish transcribing every forgotten soldier before the Atlas House falls. He stays; the book ends with the bridge reopening in spring, Silas carrying the finished ledger across it, having found a family bound not by blood but by shared remembrance.
about_author: Gideon Ravensworth is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from the First World War. He writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Silas Fairweather, POV. In a dressing station near the river valley, Silas tends the wounded and quietly enters omitted names into his leather ledger. When evacuation orders come, he measures what can be carried: ledger, morphine, one photograph. Emotional beat: quiet defiance against institutional erasure.

chapters.title: Orders to Move
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. The unit receives sudden relocation orders as shelling intensifies. Silas helps load stretchers but lingers over a dying private whose name no officer will record. He promises the man his name will survive. Emotional beat: grief sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Reaching the river crossing at dusk, Silas learns the bridge has closed for the season—floods, military decree, no exceptions. Stranded with a handful of stragglers, he accepts shelter directions to a place called Atlas House. Emotional beat: frustration curdling into uneasy hope.

chapters.title: Atlas House
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. He arrives at a crumbling mapmaking workshop run by Odile Marchand, a sharp-tongued cartographer, and meets Tomas, a nervous young man hiding a desertion. Odile offers lodging in exchange for labor. Emotional beat: wary first contact, strangers circling each other.

chapters.title: Maps of Places That No Longer Exist
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Working among drawers of obsolete maps, Silas notices villages redrawn or erased entirely—mirroring his ledger's work. Odile catches him studying them and says maps lie by omission too. Emotional beat: recognition between two keepers of lost things.

chapters.title: Tomas's Silence
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Tomas watches Silas, terrified his desertion will be reported. He reveals fragments: he fled after carrying his brother's body. Silas says nothing of the ledger but shares bread. Emotional beat: fragile trust built on mutual shame.

chapters.title: His Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. In the workshop archive, Silas finds survey notes signed with his mother's maiden name—she worked here before he was born. Confronting Odile, he learns she and his mother were close, and that Odile has letters never sent. Emotional beat: vertigo of inherited identity.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile reads aloud from her old correspondence with Silas's mother, revealing why she vanished from Silas's life: a quarrel over Silas's father and a promise broken. She confesses she watched for him for years. Emotional beat: guilt finally spoken after decades.

chapters.title: The Demolition Order
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. A military engineer arrives posting notice: Atlas House sits on land requisitioned for a supply depot; demolition comes at thaw. Odile refuses to leave. Silas realizes his ledger could document the soldiers the depot's construction would literally pave over. Emotional beat: deadline imposed on everything.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Is For
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas decides to expand the ledger into a full register of the omitted—cross-referencing workshop records, casualty lists, and the stories of stranded men passing through. Tomas reluctantly agrees to help. Emotional beat: private habit transformed into mission.

chapters.title: The Men Who Pass Through
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs. Stranded soldiers rotate through Atlas House awaiting the bridge; each carries a name someone else forgot—a brother, a friend, an enemy. Silas interviews them by lamplight. Emotional beat: the house becoming a confessional, found family forming.

chapters.title: A Raid on the Records Office
chapters.summary: Silas and Tomas, alternating POV. To verify names, they need the regimental casualty lists stored in a commandeered schoolhouse. They steal copies at night, nearly caught by a patrol. Tomas's hands shake; Silas steadies him. Emotional beat: complicity deepening friendship into brotherhood.

chapters.title: Odile's Bargain
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile trades her rarest maps to a quartermaster for time and paper, humiliating herself to protect the project. Privately she begins drafting a petition to preserve the house, using Silas's mother's name. Emotional beat: pride sacrificed for legacy.

chapters.title: The Name in the Ledger That Shouldn't Be There
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Cross-checking lists, Silas finds his own father recorded as dead—omitted from every letter home, listed under another man's error. The discovery cracks open questions about who Silas actually is. Emotional beat: identity shaken at its foundation.

chapters.title: Who Was Silas Fairweather
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile tells the full truth: Silas's father was a cartographer here, disowned, erased from the workshop's own records—the first name Odile ever failed to save. Silas rages, then understands the ledger was always his inheritance. Emotional beat: anger transmuted into belonging.

chapters.title: Frost and Betrayal
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. A passing officer recognizes Tomas and demands silence in exchange for not reporting him—payment: the stolen casualty lists. Torn, Tomas refuses and is arrested at the gate. Emotional beat: loyalty tested at terrible cost.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas testifies at Tomas's makeshift hearing, reading names from his ledger to prove deserters were men who carried others out of fire. The presiding colonel, himself unnamed in an old report, quietly dismisses the charge. Emotional beat: the ledger's power made public for the first time.

chapters.title: The Thaw Begins
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Ice groans on the river; the demolition crew arrives early. With days left, the household works around the clock copying the register onto waterproof paper while Odile hides the original maps in the cellar vault. Emotional beat: desperate, tender urgency.

chapters.title: What We Carry Across
chapters.summary: All three POVs interwoven. On the last night, they pack: Odile takes only her mother's compass, Tomas his brother's tag, Silas the finished register of four hundred and eleven names. They read the final page aloud together. Emotional beat: love declared through inventory.

chapters.title: The Wrecking Ball Waits
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. At dawn the crew foreman—an old soldier whose comrade's name is in the ledger—refuses to swing first. He delays the demolition, buying hours, then walks off the job entirely. Emotional beat: ordinary courage rippling outward from the record.

chapters.title: The Bridge Opens
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Spring floods recede; the bridge reopens. Odile chooses to stay and petition for the house; Tomas chooses to go with Silas and face whatever comes carrying proof of his brother. On the far bank, Silas mails the register to the war office and keeps the ledger. Emotional beat: bittersweet departure, family intact though scattered.

chapters.title: Names That Remain
chapters.summary: Silas, POV, years later. In a rebuilt Atlas House turned memorial archive, Silas teaches young clerks the trade of remembering. A woman arrives asking if her grandfather's name survived; Silas opens the ledger to the right page. Emotional beat: inheritance fulfilled—remembrance passed forward as a living craft.
